what_it_does: Training a very large AI model across hundreds of GPUs is enormously complex: the GPUs must constantly pass data between each other, and their computation and communication steps overlap in intricate ways that existing prediction tools get badly wrong (averaging 14% error). Lumos solves this by recording a detailed 'execution graph' from a real training run — capturing every dependency between CPU operations, GPU operations, and the synchronization signals between them — and then simulating that graph to replay or predict performance under different configurations. Tested on up to 512 NVIDIA H100 GPUs training GPT-3 variants, Lumos predicts training time with only 3.3% average error and can estimate how performance changes if you add more GPUs or resize the model, without running expensive real experiments.
method_in_detail:
The idea. When you train a giant AI model across many GPUs simultaneously, the software must split the work across machines using a combination of strategies: data parallelism (each GPU sees different data samples), pipeline parallelism (different GPUs handle different layers of the model), and tensor parallelism (individual math operations are split across GPUs). These strategies require constant coordination — GPUs send results to each other and then wait. Importantly, good implementations overlap computation with communication so neither sits idle. Getting this overlap right is hard to model because it creates complex chains of dependencies.

How it works.

Step 1 — Trace collection. Lumos uses PyTorch's built-in profiler (Kineto) to record everything that happens during one training iteration: every CPU operator, every GPU operation (called a kernel — a small GPU program that runs a specific math function), and every synchronization event. This requires only about 10 lines of added code.

Step 2 — Building the execution graph. Lumos constructs a task-level execution graph that represents every operation as a node and every ordering constraint as a directed edge. It identifies four types of edges: CPU-to-CPU (sequential operations on the same CPU thread, or cross-thread waits), CPU-to-GPU (a GPU kernel that must wait for its CPU launch command), GPU-to-CPU (a CPU synchronization event waiting for a GPU kernel to finish), and GPU-to-GPU (kernels within the same CUDA stream run sequentially; cross-stream dependencies come from event-record/wait pairs). Capturing GPU-to-GPU cross-stream dependencies is the key innovation that prior tools missed — without this, the simulated computation and communication seem to overlap more than they really do, leading to over-optimistic predictions.

Step 3 — Graph manipulation. To answer 'what if' questions without running real hardware, Lumos modifies the graph. Adding more data-parallel workers only changes communication timings. Adding pipeline stages rearranges which tasks belong to which stage and inserts new communication tasks. Changing model width or depth scales the math operation sizes.

Step 4 — Simulation. A dependency-aware event scheduler replays the graph, respecting all recorded ordering constraints, and produces a simulated trace with predicted timings for each task.

The result. Lumos achieves 3.3% average replay error across GPT-3 models from 15B to 175B parameters on 16 to 512 GPUs, compared to 14% for the prior best tool (dPRO), and accurately predicts the breakdown between exposed computation, exposed communication, and overlapped time.
